title: Safe and Scalable Collaboration in Multiagent LLM Systems: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multiagent systems are a rapidly evolving frontier of artificial intelligence that enables complex coordination, communication, and autonomous reasoning across distributed agents. This article presents a comprehensive review of multiagent LLM ecosystems, organized around four foundational pillars: coordination strategies, communication frameworks, safety challenges, and trust and alignment mechanisms. We synthesize a range of architectural approaches to agent interaction, including shared latent representations, strategic autonomy, task decomposition, and neuro-symbolic communication protocols. We then systematically examine the critical vulnerabilities distinctive to multiagent environments, namely prompt injection, perceptual adversarial attacks, reward misalignment, and operational overreach. To address these issues, we propose the trust stack: a multilayered trust framework spanning epistemic reliability, behavioral alignment, role awareness, social accountability, and institutional governance. Beyond synthesizing the literature, this review contributes a novel integrated perspective. It models the interdependencies among these four pillars, formalizes the trust stack as an operational framework with runtime-computable metrics, and derives design principles from a cross-system analysis of real multiagent deployment failures—contributions absent from prior surveys. We further investigate the prospects for superalignment through constitutional AI principles, multiagent value aggregation, and dynamic preference shaping. Collectively, this work establishes a theoretical and practical foundation for the secure, reliable, and dependable deployment of multiagent LLM systems and offers a roadmap for future research at the intersection of coordination, communication, and alignment.

title: ELLMO at LLMs4OL 2026 Tasks Flagship, Reuse, and Taxonomy: Ontology Learning Across Contexts
abstract: Ontology learning aims to transform unstructured or semi-structured information into structured representations of domain knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for automating parts of this process, but their effectiveness depends on the type of information available, including source text, partial ontologies, and related ontologies from other domains. This paper presents our submission to the LLMs4OL Challenge 2026, where we address three ontology-learning tasks: the Flagship Task, focused on ontology construction from text; the Reuse Task, focused on extending a partial ontology using text and existing triples; and the Taxonomy Task, focused on identifying taxonomic relations in a target domain using ontologies from other domains. Across these tasks, we develop task-specific methods that combine LLM prompting, NLP-based extraction, ontology context, cross-domain classification, and embedding-based downselection. Our work explores how LLM-assisted ontology-learning workflows can be adapted to different forms of textual and structured input.

title: Capability-Aware Dynamic Skill Selection for Memory-Augmented Generation
abstract: Memory-augmented large language models (LLMs) have become an important foundation for multi-turn dialogue systems, where agents are expected to recall user preferences, historical facts, and temporally evolving interaction contexts across multiple sessions. Existing memory frameworks mainly improve the storage and retrieval stages, but typically adopt a uniform read-stage paradigm in which the retrieved memory segments are directly concatenated with the current query for generation. This one-size-fits-all strategy ignores the heterogeneous nature of user queries and may lead to a "correct memory, wrong response" failure mode, where the relevant evidence is successfully retrieved but is used with an inappropriate reasoning or generation strategy.To address this limitation, we propose DySkillMem, a capability-aware dynamic skill selection framework for memory-augmented generation. DySkillMem inserts an explicit query-aware decision pathway between memory retrieval and answer generation, decoupling how to answer from how to use memory. Specifically, a Response Skill Router first classifies each query into one of five response modes, including direct answering, reasoning, contextual response, refinement, and guardrail. Then, a Memory-Use Router dynamically dispatches the query to one of four specialized memory-use skills: Temporal Reasoning, Evidence Anchoring, Multi-hop Decomposition, or a Default RAG fallback. These skills produce structured intermediate traces tailored to different memory-use patterns, thereby improving temporal grounding, factual precision, and multi-hop evidence integration. Experiments on the full LoCoMo benchmark with 1,986 QA pairs demonstrate that DySkillMem consistently outperforms Vanilla RAG under identical Top-10 retrieval settings. Across GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, DySkillMem achieves absolute accuracy gains of 6.70, 4.88, and 4.88 percentage points, respectively, with positive improvements in all model-category combinations. Ablation studies further confirm the contribution of each skill, especially Evidence Anchoring and Multi-hop Decomposition. These results show that dynamic read-stage skill selection is a model-agnostic and training-free mechanism for improving the reliability of memory-augmented LLM agents.
